summary: For ages 5–7: at the poles daylight and darkness reach extremes — in polar summer the Sun stays up even at midnight (midnight sun) and in polar winter it does not rise for weeks or months (polar night), unlike home where every day has both a sunrise and a sunset. Teach the phenomenon ('what happens'), not the axial-tilt cause (a later 7–9 topic). The central aim is for children to grasp that a single polar 'day' or 'night' can last around the full 24-hour clock — not merely a longer day than at home — and that the Sun is never switched off; in winter it simply stays hidden below the horizon.
misconceptions: The Sun is switched off in polar winter — it is still there but stays below the horizon for weeks
It is like this everywhere in winter — only near the poles do you get months with no sunrise or no sunset
Midnight sun means it is hot — the Sun stays low, so summers are still cold
Day and night vanish completely — they stretch to extremes but the yearly cycle continues
This is the same as a normal long summer day at home — the poles have the Sun up for the WHOLE 24 hours, not just longer

activities.title: Spin the day at the North Pole
steps: Move a clock hand (or a Sun marker) all the way around a full 24-hour day at the North Pole in summer, watching the Sun stay up and circle the sky without ever dipping below the horizon — at 'midnight' it is still shining and a child is playing outside

Flip a summer/winter switch and sweep the same full day again in winter: now the Sun stays hidden below the horizon the whole time, the scene stays dark, and stars and sometimes the aurora can light the sky
Say out loud, after each full turn, what the Sun did — 'it never set' in summer, 'it never came up' in winter
activities.insight: At the poles a single 'day' or 'night' can last all the way around the clock: in summer the Sun never sets and in winter it never rises — nothing like home, where morning and night always take turns.

activities.title: Home vs. pole comparison strip
steps: Look at or build a side-by-side comparison: your own normal day (a morning sunrise and an evening sunset) next to the pole's all-day-light summer and all-day-dark winter
Point to or state what is the same and what is different: at home, every day has both daytime and night-time; at the poles, light or dark can last for weeks
Finish the sentence 'At home the Sun ___ every day, but at the North Pole in summer the Sun ___.'
activities.insight: The poles are genuinely different from home: home always takes turns between day and night, while the poles can have months with no sunrise or no sunset.

activities.title: Is the Sun broken? — talk and check
steps: Answer: 'A friend says in polar winter the Sun switches off, so there is no more Sun. Is the Sun really gone or broken? What is actually happening to make it so dark?'
Explain in your own words where the Sun is during the dark polar winter
Imagine and talk about how it would feel: 'How would you sleep if it were sunny at bedtime? How would you play if it were dark all day?'
activities.insight: The Sun is never switched off in polar winter — it is still shining but stays below the horizon, so its direct light does not reach that place for weeks. The yearly light-and-dark cycle stretches to extremes but continues.

checkQuestion: At the North Pole in summer, the Sun stays up in the sky even at midnight; and in winter it's dark for weeks and the Sun doesn't come up at all. A friend says 'in polar winter the Sun switches off, or goes out, so there's no more Sun.' Is the Sun really gone or broken in the polar winter? What is actually happening to make it so dark?
checkAnswer: The Sun is NOT gone, broken or switched off — it's still shining as always. In polar winter the Sun simply stays BELOW the horizon (hidden below the edge of the ground) for weeks or months, so its light doesn't reach that spot — that's the polar night. In polar summer the opposite happens: the Sun stays ABOVE the horizon even at midnight (the midnight sun). It's very different from home, where every day has some daylight and some darkness.
